newsitem.title: UK: S&P cuts Scottish Hydro-Electric rating.
newsitem.headline: S&P cuts Scottish Hydro-Electric rating.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Tuesday it had lowered its short-term rating on Scottish Hydro-Electric Plc to A1 from A1 plus.

"The downward adjustment of Hydro-Electric's short-term rating reflects the increasing risk profile of the company's business portfolio against the background of uncertain conditions in the UK wholesale electricity markets," S&P said in a statement.

"The rating change also takes into account the potential for Hydro-Electric to move to a more highly geared financial position in accordance with the company's public statement to this effect," the agency said.
It said the rating change also took into account the potential for Hydro-Electric to move to a more highly geared financial position in accordance with the company's public statement to this effect.

"Hydro-Electric's general credit quality is based on the company's business diversity, operational strengths, and stable regulatory environment, but is offset by the increasing importance to the company of generation and supply in the competitive England and Wales market," S&P said.
"In future, higher financial leverage may result from a combination of further investment in power generation and CHP (combined heat and power) projects."

S&P said Hydro-Electric's business had regional monopolies in transmission and distribution, a low-cost, diversified generation portfolio, a growing gas trading and marketing business and a retailing operation with high local visibility and market share.

"Economic growth in the region has not had the cyclicality seen in the UK but growth prospects are limited. The company's sales are stable because of high shares of domestic and commercial consumption," the rating agency said. "Hydro-Electric is successfully exploiting supply opportunities outside its area, particularly in England and Wales, as a source of additional income."
It said the Scottish industry structure provided Hydro-Electric with a monopoly to serve all customers in the north of Scotland with load under 100 kW.

"Hydro-Electric is well-positioned to retain many of these customers after the franchise protection is removed in 1998," S&P said. "Exports to England and Wales will support substantial revenue increases in the next few years, but over time competitive pressures are likely to further reduce margins on nonfranchise sales."

S&P said generating projects currently under development included Seabank, a 50/50 joint venture with British Gas to build a 755MW plant at Bristol and Rocksavage, an agreement to take 400MW from Intergen's Rocksavage plant.

"These commitments represent incremental exposure for Hydro-Electric to both power market and financial risks, and additional generating projects in future will have the same effect," S&P said. "Over time, Hydro-Electric's incremental cost position will converge with that of new market entrants generally, diluting commercial advantages currently enjoyed from the company's low cost hydro and gas generating capacity."
"The company's strategy of assuming responsibility for power project development reduces long term production costs, while accentuating construction risk in the near term," S&P said.
It said Hydro-Electric's plans to consolidate its position in the England and Wales wholesale market entailed a substantial capital expenditure programme over the next five years.

"Hydro-Electric's financial profile is currently one of the strongest in the industry. However, the announced rating change is a forward-looking adjustment that will put the rating at a level to accommodate the general strategy that the company is likely to pursue going forward," S&P said.

"It is the view of Standard & Poor's that an A1 rating is appropriate for Hydro-Electric given the company's increasing exposure to the UK generating sector and expectations of future reductions in its financial margins and balance sheet headroom."

S&P said while Scottish Hydro-Electric's business portfolio was expected to exhibit an overall higher risk profile in future, the company nevertheless continued to benefit from low cost generation assets and a stable cash flow from its service territory in the North of Scotland.

"Over the next few weeks, Standard & Poor's will be completing reviews on other participants in the UK's wholesale power market. In light of the impending impact of 1998 deregulation and fuel/supply contract expiration, as well as the ongoing level of new entry by competitive generators, further rating adjustments may be anticipated," S&P said.
